senses.gloss:
cremation
------------------------------------------
History reveals that the disposal of the bodies of the dead has been practised by mankind in several ways: च्रेमतिओन्, बुरिअल्, consigning it to water, leaving it on mountain tops or tree tops to be devoured by animals and vultures, and embalming. Out of these the first two have been most widely practised.
In India, च्रेमतिओन् of dead bodies has been existing since very ancient days. Bodies of dvijas (‘twice-born’) (See DVIJA.) who had kept duly consecrated Vedic fires (such people were called ‘āhitāgnis’) were invariably cremated with the Vedic fires, the various wooden sacrificial vessels and implements being placed on the various limbs of the dead body, at the time of च्रेमतिओन्. Those who had not kept the Vedic fires were cremated with ordinary fire. The practice of dismembering a she-goat or a cow, technically called ‘anustaraṇī’ and keeping its various severed parts on the dead body at the time of च्रेमतिओन् was also there, but was given up in later times. (The animal was let off or gifted away.) The whole process of च्रेमतिओन् was an elaborate ritual.
Dead bodies could be carried on the shoulders by the male relatives or could be transported by a cart. According to one account, a great deal of noise is to be made by means of instruments like the cymbols, while carrying the dead body to the crematorium. Though weeping was allowed during the time of च्रेमतिओन्, it was prohibited after the च्रेमतिओन् was over.
During a period when transport and communication were difficult, people who would go out travelling either for पिल्ग्रिमगे or for business or for any other purpose, had to face many hardships. So, when someone who went out, was heard to have died (and the body could not be recovered), च्रेमतिओन् used to be done to an effigy prepared out of palāśa (Butea frondosa) leaves, flour of barley and woollen thread. This was called ‘ākṛti-दहन’ (‘burning the effigy’). Such च्रेमतिओन् of an effigy was done to people who were not heard of for twelve years or more also. If by chance they returned later, they had to undergo all the sacraments like जातकर्म, नामकरण etc.
The ashes and bones were collected after cremation—this was called ‘asthi-sañcayana’—and used to be either interred in a suitable place or consigned to a sacred river or sea.
See also ANTYEṢṬI.
